Observation: Reference model: validation MSE 358.80 kg². Used as the comparison benchmark for all neural networks.
Baseline NN reduced validation MSE compared with linear regression. Best checkpoint was epoch 41; early stopping ended training at epoch 51.
Very small learning rate; still improving at the 100-epoch limit, with high validation MSE. Consistent with slow convergence under the training budget.
Improved substantially over A01, but best performance was near the 100-epoch cap and remained worse than baseline; suggests relatively slow convergence.
Approached baseline validation performance, but required 94 epochs to reach its best checkpoint, indicating slower progress than the baseline learning rate.
Validation MSE came close to baseline but best checkpoint was reached later (epoch 85); lower learning rate may need more epochs to settle.
Reached near-baseline validation MSE by epoch 18 and stopped at 28; faster progress, with slightly worse best MSE than baseline.
Reached its best validation score very early (epoch 10); faster apparent convergence, but slightly worse MSE than baseline.
Larger learning rate produced worse validation MSE than moderate rates; oversized updates may have limited optimization quality. Confirm stability from the loss curve.
Momentum 0.5 achieved validation performance very close to baseline at an earlier best epoch (26 vs 41). The small MSE difference is not conclusive.
Momentum 0.9 reached near-baseline validation performance at epoch 21, suggesting faster convergence; result was virtually tied with momentum 0.5.
High momentum gave worse validation MSE; excessive accumulated updates may impair stability at the fixed learning rate. Inspect the curve before claiming instability.
Adam reached its best checkpoint quickly (epoch 6) but underperformed SGD at the same learning rate. This does not show Adam is generally worse at its own tuned rate.
AdamW reached best validation performance by epoch 6, but its MSE was higher than baseline; optimizer-specific learning rate/weight decay may matter.
Training with L1 achieved a slightly worse validation MSE than training with MSE. All runs were still evaluated using original-scale MSE.
Huber delta 0.5 achieved validation MSE close to baseline, with its best checkpoint at epoch 62. Delta was applied to the standardized target.
Huber delta 2.0 was the strongest alternative loss configuration among A13–A15, though still slightly worse than baseline MSE training.
Batch size 16 achieved the best validation MSE among the batch-size experiments (320.11 kg²), slightly outperforming the baseline. It reached its best checkpoint early at epoch 22.
Batch size 32 produced validation performance almost identical to the baseline (320.42 vs. 320.41 kg²). Its best checkpoint was reached at epoch 22.
Batch size 128 achieved validation MSE close to the baseline, but required 90 epochs to reach its best checkpoint and used the full 100-epoch training budget.
Increasing the batch size to 256 resulted in worse validation MSE than the baseline. The best checkpoint occurred late, at epoch 95.
Batch size 512 produced higher validation error than smaller batch sizes and did not trigger early stopping; training reached the 100-epoch limit.
Batch size 1024 further increased validation MSE. The best checkpoint was near the end of training, and the run reached the 100-epoch limit.
The largest batch size tested (2048) had the worst validation MSE among the batch-size experiments. Its best checkpoint occurred at epoch 99, and training reached the 100-epoch limit.
A single hidden layer produced worse validation MSE than the three-layer baseline. The best checkpoint was reached at epoch 50, suggesting that reducing network depth did not improve performance.
Two hidden layers achieved validation MSE very close to the baseline (320.34 vs. 320.41 kg²). Reducing depth from three layers caused no meaningful improvement.
Four hidden layers achieved the best validation MSE among the depth experiments (319.77 kg²), slightly outperforming the baseline. The best checkpoint was reached at epoch 32.

Increasing depth to six hidden layers worsened validation MSE compared with the baseline and the four-layer model. Although the best checkpoint occurred early, greater depth did not improve generalization.
Using 16 neurons per hidden layer produced the worst validation MSE among the width experiments, indicating that this narrower network performed less effectively than the baseline.
Increasing the width to 32 neurons per layer improved validation MSE compared with the 16-neuron model, but it remained worse than the baseline.
A width of 128 neurons per layer reached its best checkpoint quickly (epoch 17) and improved on the narrower networks, but its validation MSE remained slightly above the baseline.

The 256-neuron network achieved the best validation MSE among the width experiments (319.83 kg²), slightly better than the baseline. It reached its best checkpoint at epoch 21 and was the second-best Member B configuration, behind the four-layer model (B10).
